A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MSFT research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original forecasting experiments using MOIRAI, MOMENT, and UNITS, together with component ablations, sensitivity analyses, and computational measurements.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds causal data analysis, masking ablations, efficiency measurements, and cross-dataset transfer results.

M1.justification: Section 4 retains the same scale-specific adapters and LoRA, in-scale attention masking, bidirectional cross-scale aggregation, and learned prediction mixing. The added pseudocode documents this design rather than establishing an algorithmic revision.

E1.justification: The six long-sequence forecasting datasets and five tabulated probabilistic forecasting datasets are retained. Appendix D.2 adds six source-to-unseen-target transfer scenarios among the existing ETT datasets, extending evaluation to a distinct distribution-shift setting.

E2.justification: The forecasting benchmark comparators remain unchanged. The efficiency comparison expands beyond v1 Table 8's forecasting architectures: new v2 Table 9 directly compares MSFT with full finetuning, linear probing, LoRA, and AdaLoRA on computational and parameter efficiency.

E3.justification: Existing benchmark splits, forecasting horizons, model configurations, and training settings are retained. Added protocols include source-dataset finetuning followed by unseen-target evaluation, causal analysis using multiscale ETTm1 autocorrelation and embedding-norm summaries, and efficiency evaluation including parameter counts and test throughput.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands supplementary validation: Appendix C.2 tests the scale-confounding premise, Table 10 isolates aggregation without in-scale masking, Table 12 investigates knowledge forgetting through transfer, and Table 9 examines efficiency against finetuning alternatives. These address questions absent from v1's retained component and scale-sensitivity analyses.

E5.justification: v1 provides ablation point estimates without run-to-run uncertainty. v2 reports three-seed means and standard deviations in Tables 10–11 and updates Table 3 to three-run means; v1's undisclosed run count prevents inferring a particular increase. Appendix C.2 also introduces Fisher's Z-tests at alpha 0.01 and partial-correlation significance reporting.

E6.justification: Headline forecasting tables and their full appendix results are unchanged, but Table 3 contains revised ablation summaries, including MSFT's ETTm1 MSE changing from 0.353 to 0.354. Substantial new findings concern computational costs, masking interactions, and mixed transfer performance: Table 12 reports 0.470 MSE for MSFT versus 0.448 zero-shot on ETTm2-to-ETTm1 transfer. Appendix C.2 newly reports raw and scale-conditioned correlations of -0.732 and -0.481.

T1.justification: New Appendix C.1 explicitly defines the discrete scale variable and the input sample space as a union of scale-dependent Euclidean spaces. It also states that scale changes observation resolution rather than the underlying latent process. The existing backdoor-adjustment formula and method equations remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof is supplied.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: causal motivation for multiscale finetuning, the MSFT framework for encoder-based TSFMs, and improved forecasting relative to alternative finetuning and forecasting methods. No new headline contribution is introduced.

C2.justification: v2 substantially broadens interpretation and applicability discussion. It interprets the new causal analysis as supporting scale confounding, explains why aggregation can amplify unmasked attention errors, and explicitly acknowledges inconsistent transfer and lack of forgetting protection. It also evaluates higher memory use and slower training against accuracy benefits, beyond v1's general computational-cost caveat.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link and detailed training-pipeline and attention-block pseudocode in Algorithms 1–2, including padding and module-operation details. Existing optimizer and hardware disclosures remain. The added documentation has an inconsistency: Algorithm 1 labels the output projection frozen, whereas Figure 3 and Appendix D.2 describe it as trainable.

R1.justification: Appendix A.2 now distinguishes joint multiscale prediction from TTM's multiresolution pretraining and MOIRAI's multiple patch sizes, refining the novelty positioning. References to the PC algorithm and Causal-learn are added. Most forecasting-related citations and positioning remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The main narrative is largely retained. v2 rewrites Appendix A.2, introduces pseudocode, causal-analysis, and forgetting subsections, and updates appendix organization and cross-references. Smaller edits add the abstract's code-access sentence and an affiliation acknowledgment.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 9–12 and two pseudocode listings, redraws Figure 3 with its explicit attention output-projection box omitted, and reflows existing appendix tables and forecast visualizations. The other figure images and the main benchmark table structures are retained.

improvement.justification: Three-run ablation reporting, additional masking controls, and explicit transfer and efficiency limitations make the existing evidence more assessable. Pseudocode and code-access information also improve implementation transparency. These are useful extensions to an otherwise stable study, although the contradictory output-head trainability descriptions limit the documentation gain.
